sections.h: Ignatius: 'Let me be food for wild beasts'
sections.b:
Ignatius of Antioch, condemned to the beasts and taken under guard to Rome, wrote ahead to the Roman church to stop any attempt to save him. In it a condemned man speaks for himself before his death. Death is his goal: 'reach God' runs through the letter (Ignatius to the Romans 1:2; 2:1; 4:1). It is a sacrifice, wine poured out 'while an altar still stands ready' (2:2), and bread: 'I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that I may be found pure bread of Christ' (4:1). It is a birth: 'My birth is upon me' (6:1). It makes him a disciple at last: 'Now I am beginning to be a disciple' (5:3). To save him would be to 'keep me from living' (6:2).

He was already condemned and did not seek arrest. A generation later the church at Smyrna, honoring Polycarp, said 'we give no praise to people who turn themselves in' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 4:1). Irenaeus quoted 'God's wheat' as the words of one 'condemned to the beasts because of his witness toward God', and Eusebius quoted chapter 5 (Against Heresies 5.28.4; Church History 3.36).

common: Ignatius's letter to the Romans was quoted by Irenaeus, Eusebius and Jerome as the words of a martyr facing the beasts.

sections.b: Ignatius was condemned to die by wild beasts in Rome, and his letter to the Roman church is full of the arena. He calls his ten guards 'leopards' and his journey a fight with beasts, using Paul's verb from 1 Corinthians 15:32 (Ignatius to the Romans 5:1). He knows of prisoners whom the beasts were too timid to touch, and says he will coax them, or force them (5:2). He lists the deaths of the arena: 'fire and cross, battles with wild beasts, cuttings and tearings apart, scattering of bones' (5:3). Lake notes that 'leopard' here is 'the first instance of the word' in Greek or Latin literature.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 4:1-2; Ignatius to the Romans 5:1-3; 1 Corinthians 15:32; Martyrdom of Polycarp 3:1

sections.h: The church that 'presides' (Ignatius to the Romans)
sections.b: About AD 110 Ignatius of Antioch greeted the Roman church as the one that 'presides in the region of the Romans' and is 'presiding over the love', 'worthy of God' and 'named after Christ, named after the Father' (Ignatius to the Romans 1:0). He says it has 'taught others' (3:1), that Peter and Paul had given it orders (4:3), and he asks it not to use its influence to save him from the beasts (1:2; 2:1; 4:1). Catholic teaching cites the greeting for the Roman church 'which presides in charity' (Catechism 834); the Anglican scholar Lightfoot read the presidency as the church's, 'first in rank' and 'first also in love'; the Orthodox theologian Thomas Hopko as a place of honor and a 'presidency in love'. See the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:0.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 1:0; Ignatius to the Romans 3:1; Ignatius to the Romans 4:3; Ignatius to the Romans 10:2; Romans 1:8

sections.h: Peter and Paul in Ignatius to the Romans
sections.b: 'I am not commanding you as Peter and Paul did. They were apostles; I am a condemned man' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3). Ignatius assumes both apostles had taught the Roman church. Lightfoot noted that the two names are joined both in the earliest letter sent from Rome after their deaths (1 Clement 5:4-7) and in the earliest sent to it (this one). Ignatius says nothing about a bishop of Rome or about where Peter died. Eusebius makes Ignatius himself Peter's second successor at Antioch (Church History 3.36.2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 4:3; Ignatius to the Romans 1:0; 1 Clement 5:4; Matthew 16:18

sections.h: Paul's words in Ignatius to the Romans
sections.b: Ignatius borrows Paul's words for his own case: pleasing God, not people (Ignatius to the Romans 2:1; 1 Thessalonians 2:4); poured out like a drink offering (2:2; Philippians 2:17); 'not justified by that' (5:1; 1 Corinthians 4:4); 'fighting wild beasts' (5:1; 1 Corinthians 15:32); Christ's freed person (4:3; 1 Corinthians 7:22); and 'the last of them and one born at the wrong time' (9:2; 1 Corinthians 15:8-9).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 2:1-2; Ignatius to the Romans 4:3; Ignatius to the Romans 5:1; Ignatius to the Romans 9:2; 1 Corinthians 15:8-9

sections.h: 'God's bread ... the flesh of Jesus Christ' (Ignatius to the Romans)
sections.b: In the letter to the Romans Ignatius speaks of his death as bread: 'I am God's wheat ... so that I may be found pure bread of Christ' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:1). Then he says what he hungers for: 'I want God's bread, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ, who was from David's seed. And for drink I want his blood, which is love that does not decay' (7:3), echoing John 6:33 and 6:51. Lightfoot reads it of 'the union with Christ which is symbolized and pledged in the eucharist', with an indirect reference to the bread and cup like Jesus's in John 6; in his letters to the Ephesians and Smyrnaeans Ignatius speaks of the meal directly (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1). Lake notes a possible play on 'love' (agapē), a name for a church meal. On Christ's presence in the Supper, see the card at Matthew 26:26.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 4:1; Ignatius to the Romans 7:3; John 6:33; John 6:51-58; Matthew 26:26

sections.b: Written at Smyrna and dated 24 August in Lake's rendering (Ignatius to the Romans 10:1, 3), the letter asks the Roman church not to save him from the beasts. It is the only one of the seven not written to thank its readers. It gives his one title for himself in this letter, 'the overseer of Syria' (2:2), and his most famous lines: 'I am God's wheat' (4:1) and 'Now I am beginning to be a disciple' (5:3). It came down apart from the other six letters, in a tenth-century Paris manuscript printed by Ruinart in 1689 (Lake).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 1:0; Ignatius to the Romans 2:2; Ignatius to the Romans 4:1; Ignatius to the Romans 5:3; Ignatius to the Romans 10:1-3

sections.h: 'The ruler of this age' in Ignatius to the Romans
sections.b: Ignatius names the devil 'the ruler of this age', using Paul's phrase (1 Corinthians 2:6), and says he 'wants to snatch me away and ruin my mind that is set on God' (Ignatius to the Romans 7:1). The danger is not torture but rescue: anyone who helps him escape martyrdom helps the devil. At 5:3 he welcomes 'the cruel tortures of the devil' as long as he reaches Jesus Christ.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 5:3; Ignatius to the Romans 7:1; 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; John 14:30

sections.h: 'Now I am beginning to be a disciple'
sections.b: Ignatius, a bishop of many years, says he is only now beginning to be a disciple, on the road to death (Ignatius to the Romans 5:3). He will 'truly be a disciple of Jesus Christ, when the world does not even see my body' (4:2), and he wants 'not only be called a Christian but also be found one' (3:2). For him a disciple is one who follows Christ all the way to his suffering, 'an imitator of the suffering of my God' (6:3), as in Jesus's call to carry the cross (Luke 14:27).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 3:2; Ignatius to the Romans 4:2; Ignatius to the Romans 5:3; Ignatius to the Romans 6:3; Luke 14:27

sections.h: 'The overseer of Syria' and his church
sections.b: Ignatius calls himself 'the overseer of Syria' (Ignatius to the Romans 2:2), the leader of the church at Antioch, the province's capital. As he writes to Rome he leaves that church to God: 'It has God as its shepherd now, in my place. Jesus Christ alone will oversee it, along with your love' (9:1). Eusebius makes Ignatius the second in the succession from Peter to be overseer at Antioch (Church History 3.36.2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 2:2; Ignatius to the Romans 9:1; Acts 11:26

sections.b: Ignatius wrote his letter to the Romans 'from Smyrna, by the Ephesians' (Ignatius to the Romans 10:1). Eusebius says that at Smyrna, where Polycarp was, he also wrote to Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles (Church History 3.36.5).

Ignatius uses erōs, 'desire', where the New Testament never does: 'My love has been crucified, and there is no fire in me that loves material things' (Ignatius to the Romans 7:2). Lightfoot took it as 'my earthly passion', crucified as in Galatians 5:24; Origen read 'my Love' as Christ. See the note at Ignatius to the Romans 7:2.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 2:1; Ignatius to the Romans 7:2; Galatians 5:24

sections.h: The church that 'presides' (Ignatius to the Romans)
sections.b: Ignatius greets the Roman church as one that 'presides in the region of the Romans' and is 'presiding over the love' (Ignatius to the Romans 1:0), and he can call a body of believers 'the love': 'the love of the churches that welcomed me' greets the Romans (9:3). Whether 'the love' in the greeting means charity or the whole fellowship of churches, and so what kind of first place Rome holds, is read differently by Catholic teaching (Lumen Gentium 13: 'the whole assembly of charity'), the Orthodox theologian Thomas Hopko and the Anglican scholar Lightfoot: see the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:0. The letter also shows churches on his road sending people 'from city to city' to meet a prisoner (9:3).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 1:0; Ignatius to the Romans 9:3; Romans 1:8

sections.h: 'The ruler of this age' and the seen and unseen (Ignatius to the Romans)
sections.b: Ignatius takes Paul's 'rulers of this age' (1 Corinthians 2:6) in the singular for the devil: 'The ruler of this age wants to snatch me away' (Ignatius to the Romans 7:1). He prays that nothing 'seen or unseen' may envy him the death he seeks (5:3), the pair Colossians uses of all that was made in Christ, powers included (Colossians 1:16), and he welcomes 'the cruel tortures of the devil' if only he may reach Jesus Christ (5:3).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Romans 5:3; Ignatius to the Romans 7:1; 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; Colossians 1:16
